responses:
## Analysis

The current program is a binary-ladder dispatch with a 16-word unrolled block that recurses on the tail. Previous attempts only reshuffled the same logic (moving the `l == 16` check, adding comments), and they all landed at exactly 3549 cost with fitness 3.1330. That suggests the cost is dominated by the work per word, not by the control flow around it.

The one lever left in the hot path is bounds checking. In the 16-word block, each `xs[k]` carries its own bounds check (compare plus branch plus panic block), and each adds SSA instructions. If I take a 16-element subslice once, `b := xs[:16]`, the length of `b` is a constant 16, so the compiler can prove every `b[k]` in range with no per-index check. The subslice itself is a single bounds check, and it is safe because `l >= 16` guarantees `cap(xs) >= 16`.

The tail still recurses on `xs[16:]`, so behavior is unchanged, and `xs` is never written to. The rest of the ladder is left alone to keep the diff small.

I haven't run the interpreter, so the size of the gain is an estimate. The change is a semantics-preserving rewrite, so it should not affect correctness.

## Expected effect

- Removes up to 16 bounds-check compare/branch pairs per 16-word block if the prove pass did not already eliminate them. If it did, the change is neutral, which would explain why the earlier restructurings produced identical costs.
- No change to the tail ladder, correctness, or the input slice.
- Code length grows only slightly.

If this produces no change in cost, the next step would be a 32-word block that recurses less often, since call overhead per block is the other remaining cost.
